<<<SECTION:Chapter One — The Boy Who Would Learn>>>

Mr. and Mrs. Pember, of number four, Willow Drive, were proud to say that they were perfectly normal, thank you very much.

They were the last people you would expect to be involved in anything strange or mysterious, because they just did not hold with such nonsense.

Mr. Pember was the director of a firm called Grunnings, which made drills. He was a big, beefy man with hardly any neck, although he did have a very large mustache.

Mrs. Pember was thin and blonde and had nearly twice the usual amount of neck, which came in very useful as she spent so much of her time craning over garden fences, spying on the neighbors.

The Pembertons had a small son called Dudley and in their opinion there was no finer boy anywhere.

<<<SECTION:Chapter Two — The Vanishing Glass>>>

Nearly ten years had passed since the Pembertons had woken up to find their nephew on their doorstep, but Willow Drive had hardly changed at all.

The sun rose on the same tidy front gardens and lit up the brass number four on the Pembertons' front door.

It was on the corner of the quiet street that the cat was sitting as still as a statue, its eyes fixed on the far corner of Willow Lane.

Nothing like this man had ever been seen on Willow Drive. He was tall, thin, and very old, wearing long robes, a purple cloak, and high-heeled boots.

His blue eyes were light and bright and sparkling behind half-moon spectacles and his nose was very long and crooked, as though it had been broken at least twice.

"Fancy seeing you here, Professor," he said, looking at the cat. "I'd have thought you'd be teaching by now."

The cat did not answer. It simply looked at him and blinked.

"You'd better come with me. We have much to discuss, and a young wizard to protect."
